newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan firms to stay in Peru despite hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Japan firms to stay in Peru despite hostage crisis.

text.p: Japanese companies were relieved at the release of employees held for four months in captivity by Marxist guerrillas in Lima, but insisted that the traumatic incident would not alter their plans to do business in Peru.
Several companies said, however, that the crisis highlighted the need to tighten risk management procedures overseas.
"We're very relieved that this long hostage situation has been brought to a conclusion," said Hiroshi Okuda, president of Toyota Motor Corp, in a statement on Wednesday.
Peruvian troops stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence on Tuesday, freeing 71 hostages, including 24 Japanese, held by Marxist rebels since December.
Employees from a number of big Japanese firms, including Toyota, Matsushita Electric Industrial Co Ltd, NEC Corp and Mitsui Mining and Smelting Co. were among the freed Japanese hostages.

Japanese companies have a substantial presence in mineral-rich Peru, where mining concerns, exporters and other firms had invested a cumulative $764 million as of 1995, according to Japanese government figures.
Mitsui Mining, which has operated Peru's Huanzala zinc and lead mine jointly with trade house Mitsui & Co Ltd since 1964, said it will not alter its activities in Peru.
"We're not cosidering any change in our business," a Mitsui Mining spokesman said.

"But since our company's name has become well-known due to the incident, we're afraid that the risk of our firm becoming a target of terrorism may be increasing," he added. "From now on, we will seek ways to tighten our risk management."

A Toyota spokesman also said that the company will not cut back or otherwise change its operations in Peru. The giant car maker operates a truck assembly plant in Peru and has the leading market share in vehicle sales there.
Two other top Japanese car makers, Honda Motor Co Ltd and Nissan Motor Co Ltd, echoed Toyota's commitment to remain in Peru, as did electronics manufacturers Matsushita and NEC.
"We're not considering halting our investment in the country for now," Masayuki Matsushita, a Matsushita vice president, said on Wednesday.
The electronics giant makes colour televisions in Peru and has spent a total of 2.9 trillion yen ($23.0 billion) there since its first investment in 1966.
"Our current business will of course be maintained," added a spokesman for NEC, although he said the company may need to review the way it manages risk.
In 1995, Peru's exports to Japan, mostly minerals, were worth $541 million, while the country imported some $300 million worth of cars, electronics and machinery from Japan.
Peru is the leading recipient of Japanese official development loans to Latin America.
A Japanese foreign ministry spokesman said that it was too early to say whether Japan will review its aid to Peru or when it will allow travel agencies to resume offering tours to the country.
Japanese travel agencies stopped offering package tours to Peru after the rebels' attack in December. Nearly 10,000 Japanese tourists visited Peru in 1995. ($1=126 yen)
